transcript.text:
2/3 = ?/6

To change the denominator from 3 to 6, multiply it by 2. Multiply the numerator by 2 as well:

2 × 2/3 × 2 = 4/6

So the missing number is 4. Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number.
i dont get why you have to multiply both numbers by two though

You multiply both by 2 because you’re not changing the amount—just cutting the whole into smaller pieces. In 2/3, the 3 means “3 equal pieces,” and the 2 means “take 2 of them.”

With 6 pieces

To make the bottom number 6, you split each of the 3 pieces into 2 smaller pieces:

3 pieces become 6 pieces.

Each original piece now counts as 2 smaller pieces.

So the 2 pieces you had become 2 × 2 = 4 smaller pieces.

That gives:

2/3 = 4/6

Visually:

text
2/3: ■ ■ □
4/6: ■ ■ ■ ■ □ □

Both show the same shaded amount: two-thirds of the whole.

The key rule

If you only multiplied the bottom by 2, you would have:

2/6

But that is a smaller amount: 2 out of 6, not 2 out of 3. To keep the fraction the same, the top must grow by the same factor as the bottom. Mathematically, multiplying top and bottom by 2 is multiplying by 2/2, which equals 1, so the value does not change.
I still don't get why we have to multiply the top number too if we only changed the bottom one.

Because changing the bottom changes the size of each piece. If the pieces become smaller, you need more pieces to keep the same total amount.

Think of pizza
2/3

means: cut a pizza into 3 equal slices, then take 2 slices.

Now you want to describe that same pizza using 6 slices instead of 3. Each original slice must be cut in half:

text
Before: [ 1/3 ][ 1/3 ][ 1/3 ]
After: [ 1/6 ][ 1/6 ][ 1/6 ][ 1/6 ][ 1/6 ][ 1/6 ]

Your original 2 big slices have become 4 small slices:

text
2 big slices = 4 small slices

So:

2/3 = 4/6
Why the top changes

The bottom number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.

The top number tells how many of those pieces you have.

If you cut every piece into 2, you have twice as many pieces total—but you also now have twice as many pieces in your portion.

So if you only changed the bottom from 3 to 6, you would be saying:

2/6

That means 2 of the 6 small slices—only half as much pizza as before. To keep the same amount, you need 4 of the 6 slices.

Quick rule

When the bottom is multiplied by 2, the top must also be multiplied by 2 so that the fraction still represents the same amount. This is because you are multiplying by 2/2, which equals 1.

is it 4/6 because you multiply the top and bottom by 2 Next one: 2/9 + 4/9?

Yes—exactly. 2/3 = 4/6 because you multiply both the top and bottom by 2.

For the next one:

2/9 + 4/9

The bottoms are already the same (both are 9), so add only the tops and keep the bottom:

2+4/9 = 6/9

You can simplify it by dividing the top and bottom by 3:

6/9 = 2/3

So:

2/9 + 4/9 = 6/9 = 2/3

With the same denominator, you are adding pieces of the same size: 2 ninths plus 4 ninths makes 6 ninths.
I get that the answer is what you said, but I am confused about why we divide by 3 at the very end.

We divide by 3 at the end only to write the answer in its simplest form. 6/9 is correct, but both 6 and 9 can be divided by 3, so the fraction can be written more simply.

What dividing does
6/9

Both 6 and 9 are in the 3 times table:

6 ÷ 3 = 2

9 ÷ 3 = 3

So:

6/9 = 2/3

You are not changing the amount of fraction—just using bigger pieces. Six small pieces out of nine is exactly the same amount as two bigger pieces out of three.

Picture it
text
6/9: ■ ■ ■ ■ □ □ □ □ □
2/3: ■ ■ □

Both pictures show the same shaded part of the whole: two-thirds.

Why 3?

You look for a number that divides both the top and bottom. For 6 and 9, that number is 3. After dividing, 2 and 3 have no common factor except 1, so 2/3 is fully simplified.

You could leave the answer as 6/9 and it would still be mathematically correct—but 2/3 is the usual “simplest” version.
